doctrine:
**A Rule 64 petition against a COA decision must be filed within 30 days from notice. A motion for reconsideration only interrupts the period; if it is denied, the petitioner has only the remaining period, but not less than five days, from notice of the denial** (Rule 64, Section 3). A petition filed beyond that period leaves the COA decision final and executory. The Notice issued by the Commission Secretary in the form prescribed by COA Resolution No. 2013-018 (amending Section 12, Rule X of the 2009 Revised Rules of Procedure of the COA) validly communicates the Commission Proper's denial of the motion, and the remaining period runs from its receipt, not from a later COA letter answering a request for the minutes.

Reiterated: **only rank-and-file employees who are members of the collective negotiating unit are entitled to CNA incentives; high-level managerial and confidential employees (including coterminous and highly confidential employees, lawyers and executives) are not**, because they cannot become members of the negotiating unit. Their contribution to agency efficiency is immaterial (PD 1597, Section 5; EO 180, Section 3; AO 103, s. 2004, Section 3(b); PSLMC Resolution No. 4, s. 2002 and No. 2, s. 2003; AO 135, Section 2; DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1, Section 4.2). A predetermined fixed CNA incentive also violates Section 5.6 of DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1.

Applying *Madera v. COA* and *SSS v. COA* (2020): **the presumption of good faith of approving and certifying officers fails when an explicit law, rule or regulation has been violated**, so they must return the disallowed amounts; **the recipient employees must return what they received on the ground of solutio indebiti.**
facts:
On July 6, 2005, the Social Security Commission issued Resolution No. 259, s. 2005, granting (1) a P20,000.00 CNA incentive to each SSS employee covered by the collective negotiating unit as of December 31, 2004 with at least three months of prior service, and (2) a "counterpart" benefit of the same amount to SSS personnel not covered by the negotiating unit, including confidential, coterminous and contractual employees, lawyers and executives.

On post-audit, the SSS Supervising Auditor issued Notice of Disallowance No. SSS-2007-001 (2005) dated January 9, 2007, disallowing the counterpart benefit, totaling P6,180,000.00, for violating Section 3(b) of AO 103 (2004) and Section 3 of EO 180 (1987). The COA Legal Services Sector denied the SSS appeal in LSS Decision No. 2010-025 dated August 5, 2010. The COA Commission Proper En Banc denied the SSS petition for review in Decision No. 2014-069 dated May 8, 2014, which SSS received on May 15, 2014.

SSS moved for reconsideration on June 11, 2014. The Commission Proper denied it in a Resolution dated November 20, 2014, communicated through a Notice from the Commission Secretary that SSS received on February 4, 2015. On February 13, 2015, SSS asked for a certified copy of the resolution and of the minutes showing how its arguments were resolved. COA replied by letter dated March 12, 2015 that the resolution was copied verbatim in the Notice, whose format COA Resolution No. 2013-018 allows. SSS filed its Rule 64 petition on March 20, 2015, also claiming that the refusal to disclose the resolution and minutes violated due process.
issues: Whether the petition was timely filed.
Whether the COA committed grave abuse of discretion in denying the SSS motion for reconsideration through the Notice.
Whether the COA committed grave abuse of discretion in upholding the disallowance of CNA incentives granted to non-members of the negotiating unit.
Whether the approving and certifying officers and the recipient employees must return the disallowed amounts.
ruling:
**1. No. The petition was filed out of time, and the COA Decision had become final and executory.** Under Rule 64, Section 3, the petition must be filed within 30 days from notice; a motion for reconsideration interrupts the period, and upon denial the petitioner may file within the remaining period, but not less than five days, from notice of denial. SSS received the COA Decision on May 15, 2014, so its 30-day period would have ended on June 14, 2014. Its motion for reconsideration on June 11, 2014 left three days, extended to five by the Rule. Having received the Notice of denial on February 4, 2015, SSS had until February 9, 2015, but it filed on March 20, 2015, "39 days after the last day of filing."

**2. No grave abuse. The Notice validly communicated the denial and started the remaining period.** COA Resolution No. 2013-018 directs the Commission Secretary, when the Commission Proper denies a motion for reconsideration for being filed late or for failing to raise any new matter or sufficient ground, to issue a Notice informing the parties of the resolution, in the form of its Annex "A." The Notice SSS received followed that very format, "hence, there is no doubt as to its validity." SSS's rejection of the officially prescribed Notice while adopting COA's March 12, 2015 letter as its reckoning point showed its awareness that the petition was late. Even counting from March 12, 2015, SSS had only until March 17, 2015, so the March 20, 2015 filing was still late.

**3. Assuming the petition was timely, the COA did not gravely abuse its discretion in upholding the disallowance.** Judicial review of COA decisions is limited to errors of jurisdiction or grave abuse of discretion (*Madera v. COA*), and SSS failed to show that the COA ruling was not based on law and evidence. The COA applied PD 1597, Section 5 (allowances and fringe benefits require presidential approval); EO 180, Section 3 (high-level policy-making, managerial or highly confidential employees cannot join the rank-and-file organization); AO 103, Section 3(b) (new benefits suspended except CNA incentives given in strict compliance with PSLMC Resolutions No. 4, s. 2002 and No. 2, s. 2003, which grant CNA benefits only to rank-and-file employees); AO 135, Section 2; and DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1, Section 4.2 (rank-and-file employees are those who are not managerial, coterminous or highly confidential). **Taken together, high-level managerial and confidential employees are not entitled to CNA benefits because they cannot become members of the negotiating unit; "[i]t is of no moment" that they also contributed to the agency's efficiency.** The fixed P20,000.00 counterpart incentive also violated Section 5.6 of DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1, which bars predetermining the incentive amount in the CNA because it must depend on the cost-cutting measures under the CNA.

**4. Yes. The approving and certifying officers and the recipient employees are all liable to return the disallowed amounts.** The Court reviewed the statutory bases listed in *SSS v. COA* (2020) (Sections 38, 39 and 43 of the 1987 Administrative Code; Section 52, Chapter 9, Title I-B, Book V of the Administrative Code; Sections 102 and 103 of the Government Auditing Code; Section 49 of PD 1177; and Section 19 of the Manual on Certificate of Settlement and Balances) and the *Madera* rules on return. **The presumption of good faith of the approving and certifying officers "fails when an explicit law, rule, or regulation has been violated"**; the six issuances were already in force when the officers granted the benefits, so good faith could not be appreciated. **The recipients must return the payments on the ground of solutio indebiti**, as they were clearly disqualified from the incentives and the government would otherwise be prejudiced.
disposition: The petition was DISMISSED. COA Decision No. 2014-069 dated May 8, 2014 and the Resolution dated November 20, 2014 were AFFIRMED, sustaining Notice of Disallowance No. SSS-2007-001 (2005) on the P6,180,000.00 counterpart CNA benefits. The fallo does not separately order the return; the liability of the approving and certifying officers and of the recipients to return the amounts is stated in the body of the decision.

bar_questions.q: The COA Commission Proper affirmed a notice of disallowance against the Bayanihan Development Authority (BDA), a GOCC. On the 28th day after receiving the COA decision, BDA filed a motion for reconsideration. The Commission Secretary later sent BDA a one-page Notice, in the form prescribed by the COA rules, stating that the Commission Proper had resolved to deny the motion for failure to raise any new matter. BDA wrote COA asking for the full resolution and the minutes of the meeting, and COA replied by letter that the resolution is copied verbatim in the Notice. BDA filed a Rule 64 petition with the Supreme Court 30 days after receiving the Notice, and 25 days after receiving COA's reply letter. BDA argues that its period began to run only from receipt of the reply letter. (a) Was the petition filed on time? (b) Is BDA's reckoning point correct?

alac.answer: (a) No, the petition was filed out of time. (b) No, the remaining period ran from receipt of the Notice of denial, not from COA's later reply letter.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 64, Section 3 of the Rules of Court, a petition for certiorari against a COA judgment must be filed within 30 days from notice; a motion for reconsideration, if allowed, interrupts the period, and if it is denied the aggrieved party may file within the remaining period, but not less than five days, from notice of denial. Under COA Resolution No. 2013-018, amending Section 12, Rule X of the 2009 Revised Rules of Procedure of the COA, when the Commission Proper denies a motion for reconsideration for failure to raise any new matter or sufficient ground, the Commission Secretary issues a Notice in a prescribed form informing the parties of the resolution. In SSS v. COA (G.R. No. 217075, June 22, 2021), the Court held that such a Notice is valid and that the remaining period runs from its receipt; the petitioner cannot reckon the period from a later COA letter answering its request for the minutes.
alac.application: BDA used 28 of its 30 days before moving for reconsideration, leaving two days, which Rule 64 raises to five. It therefore had five days from receipt of the Notice of denial to file. Filing 30 days after receiving the Notice was far too late. The Notice followed the format prescribed by the COA rules, so it validly informed BDA of the denial. Even if the reply letter were the reckoning point, BDA would still have had only five days from its receipt, and it filed 25 days later.
alac.conclusion: The petition was filed late under either reckoning, so the COA decision had become final and executory and the petition should be dismissed.

bar_questions.q: Citing their contribution to the agency's efficiency, the governing board of a GOCC granted a fixed P25,000.00 "counterpart CNA incentive" to its department managers, lawyers and confidential staff, who are not members of the collective negotiating unit. The COA disallowed the payment, and the disallowance has become final. The board members who approved the grant and the officers who certified the vouchers claim good faith because they relied on the board resolution. The managers and lawyers who received the incentive argue that they merely received it and had no part in approving it. Who must return the disallowed amounts?

alac.answer: Both the approving and certifying officers and the recipient managers, lawyers and confidential staff must return the disallowed amounts.
alac.legal_basis: Only rank-and-file employees who are members of the collective negotiating unit are entitled to CNA incentives; high-level managerial and confidential employees are excluded under PD 1597, Section 5; EO 180, Section 3; AO 103, s. 2004, Section 3(b); PSLMC Resolution No. 4, s. 2002 and No. 2, s. 2003; AO 135; and DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1, which also prohibits predetermining the incentive amount (Section 5.6). Under the rules in Madera v. COA, approving and certifying officers who acted in bad faith, malice or gross negligence are liable to return, and recipients are liable for what they received unless an exception applies. In SSS v. COA (G.R. No. 217075, June 22, 2021), the Court held that the presumption of good faith of approving and certifying officers fails when an explicit law, rule or regulation has been violated, and that recipient employees must return disallowed CNA incentives on the ground of solutio indebiti.
alac.application: The incentive went to employees outside the negotiating unit, in violation of the issuances above, all of which were already in force, and it was a predetermined fixed amount. The officers' reliance on their own board resolution cannot sustain good faith because the grant violated explicit laws and regulations, and the recipients' contribution to efficiency is immaterial. The recipients, though passive, were clearly not entitled to the incentive and received it by mistake, so they must return it under solutio indebiti; otherwise the government would be prejudiced.
alac.conclusion: The approving and certifying officers and all the recipients are liable to return the disallowed counterpart CNA incentives.

bar_questions.q: Atty. Reyes is a department manager of a government financial institution whose duties are managerial and highly confidential. He applied for membership in the accredited rank-and-file employees' organization so that he could share in the CNA incentive under its collective negotiation agreement. (a) May he join the organization? (b) If the institution instead pays him an amount equal to the CNA incentive, is the payment valid?

alac.answer: (a) No. As a high-level employee, he is not eligible to join the organization of rank-and-file employees. (b) No. The payment is invalid and may be disallowed.
alac.legal_basis: Section 3 of EO 180 provides that high-level employees whose functions are normally considered policy-making or managerial or whose duties are of a highly confidential nature shall not be eligible to join the organization of rank-and-file government employees. Under AO 103, s. 2004, Section 3(b); PSLMC Resolution No. 4, s. 2002 and No. 2, s. 2003; AO 135; and DBM Budget Circular No. 2006-1, Section 4.2, CNA incentives may be granted only to rank-and-file employees, defined as those who are not managerial, coterminous or highly confidential. In SSS v. COA (G.R. No. 217075, June 22, 2021), the Court held that high-level managerial and confidential employees are not entitled to CNA benefits because they cannot become members of the negotiating unit, and upheld the disallowance of "counterpart" CNA benefits paid to them.
alac.application: Atty. Reyes performs managerial and highly confidential functions, so EO 180 bars him from the rank-and-file organization. Because CNA benefits arise from membership in the negotiating unit, he cannot share in the CNA incentive, and paying him an equivalent "counterpart" amount would do indirectly what the law forbids. As in SSS v. COA, the COA may disallow the payment, and he would have to return what he received.
alac.conclusion: Atty. Reyes may neither join the rank-and-file organization nor validly receive the CNA incentive or its equivalent.

notes: The petition was dismissed mainly for late filing; the rulings on the merits and on the liability to return were made on the assumption that the petition had been timely filed. The decision relies on Madera v. COA (G.R. No. 244128, September 8, 2020) and SSS v. COA (G.R. No. 244336, October 6, 2020). Leonen, J. was on official leave.
